what_its_for: Axitinib is a cancer medicine used to treat advanced kidney cancer (also called renal cell carcinoma) in adults. It works by blocking certain proteins that help tumors grow and form new blood vessels, which slows or stops the cancer from spreading.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablet whole with a glass of water. You can take it with or without food. Try to take it at the same times every day, about 12 hours apart (for example, once in the morning and once in the evening). Do not crush, chew, or split the tablets.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 5 mg taken twice a day (every 12 hours). Your doctor may adjust your dose up or down depending on how well you tolerate the medicine and how it is working for you. Always take the exact dose your doctor prescribes — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next scheduled dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at once or take an extra dose to make up for the one you missed. If you vomit after taking a dose, do not take another dose — just wait and take your next regular dose.
storage: Store axitinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Store in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a safe drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges (found in some marmalades) while taking this medicine — they can increase the amount of drug in your body and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid St. John's Wort, a herbal supplement, as it can make axitinib less effective. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting axitinib, as many drugs can interact with it. Avoid becoming pregnant while on this medicine — use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 week after your last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking axitinib.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: very high blood pressure or a sudden severe headache; chest pain, shortness of breath, or signs of a heart attack or stroke (sudden numbness, weakness, confusion, or trouble speaking); coughing up blood or blood in your stool or urine; severe stomach pain; wound healing problems; signs of a blood clot (leg pain, swelling, redness); extreme tiredness or fatigue; severe skin reactions or blistering; vision changes; signs of thyroid problems (unusual weight gain or loss, feeling very cold or hot, hair loss). Also call your doctor if you have ongoing diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, or mouth sores that are hard to manage.
when_it_works: Axitinib starts working in your body right away, but it may take several weeks to months before your doctor can tell if the medicine is controlling your cancer through scans and tests. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor, even if you do not feel any different. Keep all your follow-up appointments so your doctor can monitor how well the medicine is working.
special_populations: Liver problems: Your doctor may start you on a lower dose if you have moderate liver disease. Axitinib is not recommended if you have severe liver disease. Kidney problems: No dose adjustment is usually needed for kidney problems alone, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Older adults (65 years and older): Axitinib can be used in older adults, but you may be more sensitive to side effects such as high blood pressure and fatigue — your doctor will watch you carefully. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Axitinib can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 1 week after stopping. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use contraception during treatment and for at least 1 week after stopping. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Children: Axitinib is not approved for use in children.
